title: Kosovo Joins International Force for Gaza: A Step Toward Peace or More Complications?
summary:
In a significant diplomatic development, Kosovo has formally agreed to join the International Stabilization Force (ISF) in Gaza, a US-led multinational mission mandated by the United Nations to maintain stability in the Palestinian enclave after the recent war.

The agreement was signed on Monday by Kosovo Security Force Commander Lieutenant-General Bashkim Jashari and US ISF Commander Major-General Jasper Jeffers, according to a statement from the US-backed Board of Peace. The accord underscores Kosovo's commitment to President Donald Trump's 20-point peace plan, which was introduced a year ago to end the conflict.

The ISF is envisioned as a multinational security mission that will manage demilitarization, train a Palestinian police force, and oversee security in post-conflict Gaza. Kosovo joins a short list of contributing nations, including Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Albania, and Uganda. Notably, Turkey will not participate after Israel vetoed its involvement.

However, the deployment of the ISF has encountered roadblocks. Disagreements persist over the timing of Israel's military withdrawal from Gaza and the disarmament of Hamas. Nikolay Mladenov, high representative for the Board of Peace, emphasized that Israel must implement its commitments under the peace roadmap for progress to be made. "We are still at the point at which we need to make sure that what has been agreed is going to be implemented and is going to change significantly the lives of the people in Gaza," he said. "Unfortunately, we're not there yet."

Despite these challenges, the US has committed over $206 million to support the ISF, with funds allocated for equipment, infrastructure, vehicles, and operational costs. An additional $6 million will repurpose US armored vehicles for the force.

Kosovo's participation marks a notable expansion of the coalition, reflecting the international community's investment in stabilizing Gaza. Yet, the success of the mission hinges on resolving the thorny issues that remain. As Mladenov noted, discussions are ongoing, but the path forward is far from certain.
why_it_matters: For readers who will inherit this region's unresolved conflicts, the story shows how complicated it is to build peace after a war: new countries joining a mission does not mean the hard parts are solved. It also explains why headlines about Gaza may keep shifting, because agreements remain fragile until both sides carry out uncomfortable promises.

background_read: Kosovo is a small, mostly Albanian-speaking country in southeastern Europe that declared independence from Serbia after years of conflict; its security force is much smaller than a traditional army.
Gaza is a narrow strip of Palestinian land on the Mediterranean coast where the militant group Hamas has long governed, and repeated wars with Israel have left much of the territory in ruins.
The US-backed Board of Peace mentioned in the article is the body overseeing the current peace plan, with high representative Nikolay Mladenov helping to handle negotiations.
Turkey's absence matters because Turkey is a powerful regional country that supports Palestinians, and Israel did not trust it to remain neutral, leading to the veto.

Multinational peacekeeping missions look strong on paper, but they struggle when the parties involved will not agree on timing or disarmament. Earlier peace efforts in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict show that money and good intentions cannot replace actual commitments by the warring sides.

perspectives.description: Kosovo's contribution broadens the international footprint of the ISF and signals that the peace plan has support beyond just the US and Israel. More contributors also mean more resources and less burden on any single country.

The ISF can only succeed if Israel follows its withdrawal commitments and Hamas gives up weapons. The quote from Mladenov suggests that even with money and troops, the mission may be stalled, and civilians in Gaza remain stuck in uncertainty.

Small countries like Kosovo often join international missions not only for altruism but also to build alliances and gain security ties with powerful partners such as the United States. Their participation can be as much about their own foreign policy as about helping Gaza.

perspectives.perspective: A test for the peace plan
perspectives.description: The next few months will reveal whether the promised withdrawal and demilitarization actually happen, and whether Palestinian police can take control without sparking new fighting. If the mission succeeds, it may set a model; if it fails, countries may withdraw and another ceasefire could collapse.
